kurals.tamil:
நினைத்தொன்று சொல்லாயோ நெஞ்சே எனைத்தொன்றும்
எவ்வநோய் தீர்க்கும் மருந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Ninaiththondru sollaayo nenje enaiththondrum
evvanoai theerkkum marundhu.
kurals.meaning: O my heart, will you not think it over and tell me some medicine, any medicine at all, that can cure this grief-sickness nothing else can cure?
kurals.elementary: Imagine you miss someone so much that it feels like a tummy ache that no medicine can fix. So you talk to yourself: “Come on, heart, you are clever, think of something that will make me feel better!”
kurals.university: Chapter 125, neñcoṭu kiḷattal (‘speaking with one’s heart’), belongs to the kaṟpiyal (wedded-love) section: the wife, alone in separation (pirivu), turns her own neñcu (heart/mind) into a confidant and argues with it, a device Pope renders ‘Soliloquy’. The key compound evvanōy joins evvam (‘distress, sorrow’) with nōy (‘disease’), and enaittonṟum (‘whatever it may be, of any kind’) stresses that she will accept any remedy at all; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the sickness as grown out of love (காதலால் வளர்ந்த), and Kalaignar as kātal nōy ‘incurable by any medicine’. The commentary tradition reads the opening ninaittu onṟu collāyō as a plea to the heart, the one faculty still ‘with’ her, to think on her behalf. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the chapter title is printed as one word (நெஞ்சொடுகிளத்தல்) on ytamizh and as நெஞ்சோடு கிளத்தல் (long ō) on thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “I can find no means to drive away this grief which is drying up my senses.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna, overwhelmed by sorrow, confesses that nothing he can think of will remove the grief that is withering him, and turns to Krishna for a remedy.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine likewise admits her grief is beyond ordinary cures and begs her own heart to find the medicine.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.8 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com (first sentence of 2.8); strong match on a grief with no known remedy, though Arjuna’s sorrow is moral and martial, not the ache of a lover.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Why is my pain perpetual, and my wound incurable, which refuseth to be healed?”
christianity.explanation: Jeremiah cries out that his inner wound will not heal no matter what is tried.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ‘sickness no medicine cures’, Jeremiah’s pain is described as incurable, prompting a desperate question.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); close on the incurable inner wound, but the prophet’s anguish comes from persecution and his calling, not love.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when I am ill, it is He who cures me”
islam.explanation: Abraham names God as the one true healer of every illness.
islam.tie_back: Where the Kural’s heroine searches her own heart for a cure, the Qur’an points the sufferer to God as the source of healing.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); shares the question of who can cure an affliction, but the verse concerns illness in general, not love-sickness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? Why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered?”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah asks, in grief, why no remedy or healer seems able to cure his people’s wound.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s plea for ‘any medicine at all’ echoes this famous lament asking whether any balm exists for an aching heart.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); strong rhetorical parallel of searching for a remedy, though the sufferer is a nation, not a lover.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha diagnoses grief as springing from attachment to the dear, and names freedom from attachment as its only real cure.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural asks for a medicine for love-grief; the Dhammapada answers that the cure lies in loosening the endearment itself.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it answers the Kural’s question directly, though its remedy (detachment) is one the heroine would refuse.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The mind of those who always live in unfrequented lodgings, who eat low food, and who subdue their senses, will not be attacked by the foe, Love, who is vanquished as disease is by medicine.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira’s teaching treats Love as an enemy-sickness and prescribes the discipline of the senses as its medicine.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural asks what medicine can cure love-sickness; the Uttaradhyayana names one, though it is the monk’s cure of renunciation, not the lover’s cure of reunion.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi, Lecture 32); the ‘love as disease, discipline as medicine’ image matches, but the Jain cure ends love rather than satisfying it.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The poet Theocritus tells of the Cyclops Polyphemus, hopelessly in love with the sea-nymph Galatea, and opens by saying there is no other remedy for love, neither ointment nor salve, except the Muses; Polyphemus eased his love by sitting on a rock and singing to her.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Idyll treats love as an illness with almost no cure, and finds relief only in song, a kind of talking to oneself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine likewise looks for a medicine for love and, finding none, pours her heart out in words to herself.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory of a well-known poem, not verified against a live text this session; a near match on ‘no medicine for love’ and soliloquy as relief.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero, discussing the passions, sets out the ‘cure’ for love: show the lover how trivial the object of desire is, turn his mind to other cares and interests, and sometimes treat it like other illnesses by change of place.
philosophy.explanation: Cicero treats erotic love as a disturbance of the mind that philosophy can treat like a disease.
philosophy.tie_back: Where the Kural’s heroine begs for any medicine for love-sickness, Cicero offers a philosopher’s prescription.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory, not verified live this session; Cicero does discuss remedies for love in Book 4, but section numbers should be treated as approximate.

kurals.tamil:
காதல் அவரிலர் ஆகநீ நோவது
பேதைமை வாழியென் நெஞ்சு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaadhal avarilar aakanee noavadhu
paedhaimai vaazhiyen nenju.
kurals.meaning: Long live you, my heart! Since he has no love for us, your suffering over him is simply foolishness.
kurals.elementary: Imagine you keep waiting by the door for a friend who has forgotten all about you. You might say to yourself, “Silly heart, why are you sad about someone who isn’t even thinking about you?”
kurals.university: The heroine now scolds her heart: kātal avar ilar āka (‘he being without love’), nī nōvatu (‘your aching’) is pētaimai (‘folly, simple-mindedness’, from pētai ‘simpleton’). The interjection vāḻi eṉ neñcu (‘long may you live, my heart!’) is a conventional blessing that here carries gentle irony, as Solomon Pappaiah’s rendering ‘நீ வாழ்ந்து போ’ makes explicit. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both gloss pētaimai as aṟiyāmai (ignorance), and Pope translates ‘thy smart is folly, fare thee well my heart’. The traditional reading, which modern commentators follow, takes the accusation of lovelessness as the wife’s overstatement in grief rather than a settled judgment of her husband. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “For him who has conquered the mind, the mind is the best of friends; but for one who has failed to do so, his very mind will be the greatest enemy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that the mind can be either one’s closest ally or one’s worst foe, depending on whether it is mastered.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine discovers this double nature: her heart is both her only confidant and the foolish source of her pain.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.6 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com; fits the chapter’s self-address to the mind, but the Gita speaks of yogic self-mastery, not unrequited love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs urges a person to guard the heart carefully, since everything in life flows from it.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine, seeing her heart ache foolishly, is in effect trying to keep watch over it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a general instruction to guard the heart, with no reference to unreturned love.

islam.quote_or_event: “But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you; and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allah Knows, while you know not.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns that what the heart loves is not always good for it, since human knowledge is limited.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine tells her heart that loving one who does not love back is folly, a love that is ‘bad for you’.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih), quoting the verse’s second half; the verse’s context is fighting, so the application to love is thematic only.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Why art thou cast down, O my soul? And why moanest thou within me? Hope thou in God; for I shall yet praise Him for the salvation of His countenance.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist questions his own downcast soul as if it were another person, challenging its sorrow.
judaism.tie_back: This is the same inner dialogue the Kural stages: the speaker addresses her heart and asks why it aches.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917; 42:5 in Christian numbering); a strong formal match for speaking to one’s own soul, though the longing is for God.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A fool who knows his foolishness is wise at least to that extent, but a fool who thinks himself wise is a fool indeed.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that recognising one’s own foolishness is already the beginning of wisdom.
buddhism.tie_back: By calling her own heart foolish (pētai), the Kural’s heroine shows exactly this first glimmer of self-knowledge.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; connects on self-recognised folly, but the verse is about spiritual ignorance, not love.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If you owned the beauty of Vaiśramaṇa, the pleasing manners of Nalakūbara, if you were like Purandara himself, I should have no desire for you.”
jainism.explanation: Rājīmatī, now a nun, tells Rathanemi, who has fallen for her, that his longing is hopeless and recalls him to his vows.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine tells her heart the same hard truth: aching for someone who does not return your love is folly.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi, Lecture 22; diacritics normalised); the episode shows the folly of unreturned longing, but from the side of the one who refuses, in a monastic setting.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Back in his own palace, Odysseus lies awake seething, strikes his breast and rebukes his own heart, telling it to endure, since it once endured something worse, the day the Cyclops devoured his companions.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows a hero talking sternly to his own heart (kradiē) to master an overwhelming emotion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Odysseus speaks to his heart as to a separate person, reproaching it for what it feels.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified live (a Gutenberg fetch was truncated); a famous instance of addressing one’s heart, though Odysseus’s emotion is anger, not love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal observes that the heart has its own reasons, which reason does not know.
philosophy.explanation: Pascal sees the heart as a faculty that loves and judges by its own logic, often against what reason advises.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine faces exactly this: her reason calls the heart’s ache folly, yet the heart goes on aching.
philosophy.source: Blaise Pascal, Pensées, no. 277 (Brunschvicg numbering; 423 in Lafuma) (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous saying; the live fetch did not reach the passage, so wording is not quoted. Good fit on heart versus reason, though Pascal applies it chiefly to faith.

kurals.tamil:
இருந்துள்ளி என்பரிதல் நெஞ்சே பரிந்துள்ளல்
பைதல்நோய் செய்தார்கண் இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Irundhulli enparidhal nenje parindhullal
paidhalnoai seydhaarkan il.
kurals.meaning: My heart, why stay here thinking of him and suffering? The one who gave us this sickness of sorrow has no tender thought for us.
kurals.elementary: Think of sitting by the window all day thinking about a friend who moved away, while that friend is busy and not thinking about you. You might ask yourself, “Why am I sitting here feeling sad when they aren’t even missing me?”
kurals.university: The heart is questioned for sitting idle: iruntu uḷḷi (‘remaining here and thinking’) eṉ paritaltal (‘why grieve?’), while parintu uḷḷal (‘thinking with tender pity’) is absent in the one who caused paital nōy (‘the sickness of sorrow’; paital = distress). Solomon Pappaiah unpacks iruntu as ‘neither going to where he is, nor dying here’, a reading that sharpens the reproach of passive pining. Pope’s explanation on ytamizh.com prints ‘there are no lewd thoughts (of you) in him’, which looks like a transcription slip for ‘loving thoughts’; all four Tamil glosses render parintu uḷḷal as anpu or irakkam (love, pity). The commentary tradition treats the line as the heroine voicing a suspicion she does not finally believe. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “While speaking learned words, you are mourning for what is not worthy of grief.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna gently rebukes Arjuna for indulging a grief that true understanding would not sustain.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine rebukes her heart in the same way: why sit here grieving over one who is not grieving for you?
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.11 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com (first sentence of 2.11); the reproach of needless grieving fits, but Krishna’s reason (the soul’s immortality) is unrelated to love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs observes that waiting endlessly for what one longs for makes the heart literally ill.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sits pining for a husband who does not come, and names her state a ‘sickness of sorrow’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a close match on longing as heart-sickness, though it lacks the Kural’s note of one-sided love.

islam.quote_or_event: “Those who have believed and whose hearts are assured by the remembrance of Allah. Unquestionably, by the remembrance of Allah hearts are assured.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that the heart finds true rest in remembering God.
islam.tie_back: In contrast to the Kural’s heart, which finds only sickness in dwelling on an absent man, the Qur’an names a remembrance that brings peace.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a contrastive rather than direct parallel about what the remembering heart should dwell on.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Return, O my soul, unto Thy rest; For the LORD hath dealt bountifully with thee.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist tells his own soul to stop its restless distress and come back to rest.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine likewise tells her heart to stop sitting and pining in vain.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); same form of self-address, but the psalmist’s reason for calm is God’s kindness, not the beloved’s indifference.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seek no intimacy with the beloved and also not with the unloved, for not to see the beloved and to see the unloved, both are painful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha notes that being apart from a loved one is itself a form of suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is living exactly this pain of ‘not seeing the beloved’.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; names separation from the beloved as pain, though the Buddha’s advice (avoid attachment) differs from the heroine’s.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra lists ārta-dhyāna, ‘sorrowful brooding’, as an inauspicious form of meditation, one kind being the constant thought of regaining a cherished person or thing from which one has been separated.
jainism.explanation: Jain psychology classes repeated grieving over a lost beloved as a harmful mental state that binds karma.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine, ‘sitting and thinking’ of the husband who has gone, is caught in exactly this kind of brooding, which her own heart questions.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra ch. 9, sutras on ārta-dhyāna (tr. Nathmal Tatia, paraphrase; sutra numbers differ between Svetambara and Digambara recensions)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from knowledge of a standard doctrine, not verified live this session; close conceptual match, though Jainism condemns the brooding the Kural sympathetically portrays.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ariadne, waking on the island of Naxos to find Theseus has sailed away, writes to him from the shore, lamenting that she still thinks of him while he has no thought or pity for her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid gives voice to an abandoned heroine whose love is met only by the beloved’s indifference.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine, too, sits grieving for one who ‘has no tender thought’ for her.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known poem, not verified live; Theseus’s desertion is deliberate, whereas the Kural’s husband is only away.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus begins his handbook by dividing things into those within our power, such as our judgments and desires, and those not within our power, which we must not let disturb us.
philosophy.explanation: Stoic practice trains the mind to stop agonising over what lies in another’s control.
philosophy.tie_back: Whether the absent husband thinks of her is not in the heroine’s power, which is why her reason questions her heart’s pining.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the opening of the Enchiridion, not verified live; it offers a Stoic remedy for the situation rather than a parallel to the heroine’s feeling.

kurals.tamil:
கண்ணும் கொளச்சேறி நெஞ்சே இவையென்னைத்
தின்னும் அவர்க்காணல் உற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Kannum kolachchaeri nenje ivaiyennaith
thinnum avarkkaanal utru.
kurals.meaning: My heart, when you go to him, take my eyes along with you; longing to see him, they are eating me alive.
kurals.elementary: Imagine your heart can fly to visit someone you miss, but your eyes are stuck at home and keep crying because they want to see that person too. So you say, “Heart, please take my eyes with you, they won’t stop bothering me!”
kurals.university: This couplet presupposes that the heart has already gone to the absent husband (a convention developed in neighbouring couplets), so the heroine asks it to take the eyes too: kaṇṇum koḷa (‘taking the eyes also’) cēṟi (‘you will go’). The eyes, left behind, ivai eṉṉait tiṉṉum (‘these devour me’) avar kāṇal uṟṟu (‘set on seeing him’); Mu. Varadarasanar glosses tiṉṉum as பிடுங்கித் தின்கின்றன (‘pluck and eat’), and Pappaiah softens it to ‘grieve as though eating me’. The image of a body divided against itself, heart travelling while eyes torment the one who stays, extends the Kāmattuppāl motif of personified eyes (compare chapter 118, kaṇ vitumpu aḻital). Pope renders the line ‘O rid me of these eyes, my heart’. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When You go off to the forest during the day, a tiny fraction of a second becomes like a millennium for us because we cannot see You.”
hinduism.explanation: The gopis tell Krishna that every moment their eyes cannot see him is unbearable.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine likewise suffers through her eyes, which torment her with their craving to see the absent beloved.
hinduism.source: Srimad Bhagavatam 10.31.15 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io (first sentence of the translation); a strong viraha match centred on the eyes’ hunger to see the beloved.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Mine eyes fail for thy word, saying, When wilt thou comfort me?”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist describes his eyes wearing out with longing as he waits for a comfort that does not come.
christianity.tie_back: In the Kural the eyes, too, are consumed by longing for one who stays away.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); good match on eyes failing with longing, though the object of longing is God’s promise.

islam.quote_or_event: “For indeed, it is not eyes that are blinded, but blinded are the hearts which are within the breasts.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an distinguishes the eyes from the heart and locates true seeing in the heart.
islam.tie_back: The Kural also separates eyes and heart, imagining the heart going off while the eyes stay behind and suffer.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih), quoting the verse’s second sentence; only the eyes-and-heart pairing connects, as the verse is about spiritual blindness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I am weary of my crying; my throat is dried; Mine eyes fail while I wait for my God.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist describes his eyes worn out with waiting and weeping for one who has not yet come.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes are similarly ‘eaten up’ by waiting to see the absent beloved.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917; 69:3 in Christian numbering); strong physical image of eyes failing in longing, though directed to God.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The monk Vakkali loved simply to gaze at the Buddha’s body; when he was ill and longed to see him, the Buddha came and told him that there was no point in looking at this body, for whoever sees the Dhamma sees the Buddha.
buddhism.explanation: The story treats the eyes’ craving to see a beloved form as something to be redirected inward.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes are consumed by the same craving to see the beloved, which the Buddha gently tells Vakkali to look beyond.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known sutta; the live page did not load this session. Strong match on longing eyes, though Vakkali’s devotion is to a teacher, not a spouse.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is passionately fond of ‘colours,’ will come to untimely ruin; just as an impassioned moth which is attracted by the light rushes into death.”
jainism.explanation: In Jain teaching each sense, beginning with the eye, can destroy a person through its passionate attachment to its object.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes, ‘eating’ the heroine with their craving to see her husband, are just such a sense consuming its owner.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi, Lecture 32); good match on the eye’s craving as self-destructive, though Jainism prescribes giving up the craving.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Clytie, abandoned by the sun-god Helios, sat on the bare ground for nine days without food, turning her face and eyes to follow him across the sky, until she was changed into a flower that still turns toward the sun.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s story makes the abandoned lover’s gaze itself the thing that consumes her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s eyes, which ‘eat’ the heroine in their longing to see her husband, Clytie’s eyes follow her beloved until she wastes away.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not verified live; line numbers approximate. A close image of eyes fixed on an absent beloved.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Phaedrus, Socrates describes how the lover’s soul, when parted from the beloved, becomes parched and frantic, unable to sleep or rest, and runs wherever it hopes to catch sight of the beautiful one, finding relief only in seeing him.
philosophy.explanation: Plato treats the sight of the beloved as what nourishes the lover’s soul, and its absence as torment.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes, tormenting the heroine in their need to see her husband, express the same dependence on sight.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from knowledge of the passage, not verified live; a strong thematic match on the torment of not seeing the beloved.

kurals.tamil:
செற்றார் எனக்கை விடல்உண்டோ நெஞ்சேயாம்
உற்றால் உறாஅ தவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Setraar enakkai vidtalundo nenjaeyaam
utraal uraaa thavar.
kurals.meaning: My heart, though he does not come to us even when we long for him, can we really give him up, saying “he hates us”?
kurals.elementary: Imagine a friend who hasn’t called you back in a long time. You could decide, “They don’t like me anymore, I’ll forget them,” but deep down you know you can’t stop caring about them.
kurals.university: The heroine tests the idea of abandoning her husband and rejects it: ceṟṟār eṉa (‘saying he is one who hates us’, from ceṟu ‘to hate, be hostile’) kaiviṭal uṇṭō (‘is there such a thing as letting go?’). The second line contrasts yām uṟṟāl (‘though we draw close, long for him’) with uṟāatavar (‘he who does not draw close’), the lengthened uṟāa being an alapeṭai (prosodic lengthening) for metre. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the question as rhetorical (‘can we give him up?’), whereas Pappaiah turns it toward her own will (‘do I have the firmness of heart to give him up?’). The couplet thus marks the chapter’s turn from reproaching the heart to confessing its constancy. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “So let us give up all friendship with this dark-complexioned boy, even if we can’t give up talking about Him.”
hinduism.explanation: In the ‘Song of the Bee’, the gopis, feeling abandoned by Krishna, list his apparent cruelties and resolve to give him up, yet admit they cannot stop speaking of him.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine reaches the same impasse: she can call him unloving, but she cannot let him go.
hinduism.source: Srimad Bhagavatam 10.47.17 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io (final sentence of the translation); a near one-to-one match on being unable to abandon a seemingly indifferent beloved.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes true love as something that does not give up, however much it must endure.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds her love for her absent husband cannot be abandoned, even when he seems not to return it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); fits love’s refusal to give up, though Paul describes agape, not a wife’s romantic longing.

islam.quote_or_event: “…he has impassioned her with love. Indeed, we see her [to be] in clear error.”
islam.explanation: The women of the city say that the governor’s wife is so consumed with love for Joseph, who does not return it, that she has lost all judgment.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, she loves one who does not draw near to her and cannot give that love up.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih), quoting only the verse’s latter part; the unreturned, unshakable love matches, but the Qur’an frames her passion as wrongful, unlike the Kural’s faithful wife.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Many waters cannot quench love, Neither can the floods drown it; If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, He would utterly be contemned.”
judaism.explanation: The Song of Songs declares that love, once kindled, cannot be put out by any force.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds that even the thought ‘he hates us’ cannot quench her love.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a strong match on love’s refusal to be extinguished, though without the Kural’s unresponsive partner.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Therefore hold nothing dear, for separation from the dear is painful. There are no bonds for those who have nothing beloved or unloved.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that holding someone dear creates a bond that makes separation painful.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine discovers just such a bond: she cannot let go of the one she holds dear, even though it hurts.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it explains why she cannot let go, but recommends the very detachment she rejects.

jainism.quote_or_event: The courtesan Kośā loved Sthūlabhadra, who left her to become a monk; when he returned years later to spend a rainy season in her house, he did not return her love, yet her devotion did not die, and in the end she was won over to the Jain path herself.
jainism.explanation: This famous Jain story shows a woman whose love outlasts the beloved’s withdrawal, until it is transformed rather than abandoned.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Kośā cannot simply give up the one who no longer draws near to her.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Pariśiṣṭaparvan, story of Sthūlabhadra and Kośā (paraphrase)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested Jain narrative, not verified live this session; the constancy matches, but the story’s point is the monk’s chastity and Kośā’s conversion.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The nymph Echo, rejected by Narcissus, hides in the woods in shame, yet her love clings to her and even grows with the pain of being refused.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid portrays a love that survives open rejection and cannot be torn out.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds the same: even if he does not come to her, she cannot cast her love aside.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage (‘et tamen haeret amor crescitque dolore repulsae’), not verified live; line numbers approximate. Close on enduring unreturned love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle asks whether a friendship should be broken off when the other person changes, and answers that one should not break it off hastily, but keep some regard for the friend for the sake of the past.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that a bond once formed should not be lightly abandoned even when the other has changed.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine reaches a similar conclusion about her husband: she cannot write him off as one who hates her.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from knowledge of the chapter, not verified live; a reasoned parallel about not breaking bonds, though Aristotle discusses friendship, not marital love.

kurals.tamil:
கலந்துணர்த்தும் காதலர்க் கண்டாற் புலந்துணராய்
பொய்க்காய்வு காய்திஎன் நெஞ்சு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kalandhunarththum kaadhalark kandaar pulandhunaraai
poikkaaivu kaaidhi-en nenju.
kurals.meaning: My heart, when you see the beloved who ends our quarrels by embracing us, you cannot even sulk; so this anger you now show him is false.
kurals.elementary: Imagine pretending to be cross with your best friend, but the moment they come and give you a hug, you start smiling. So you tell yourself, “I’m not really angry, I’m just pretending!”
kurals.university: The couplet turns on the Tamil love-poetry concept of ūṭal / pulavi (a lover’s feigned sulking that is meant to be dissolved): the husband is one who kalantu uṇarttum (‘removes the sulk by union’), and when the heart sees him it does not pulantu uṇar (‘sulk and then make up’) at all. Hence its present anger is poykkāyvu (‘false heat, sham anger’, from kāy ‘to burn, be angry’) that it kāyti (‘burns with’). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan follow this reading closely, while Solomon Pappaiah expands it into an exhortation: ‘give up this pretended hatred and go to him’. The couplet anticipates the later chapters on pulavi (131-133). Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (both read kaṇṭāṟ with the sandhi ṟ).

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda, Radha, hurt by Krishna’s wandering, holds herself aloof in proud anger (mana), and her friend urges her not to be harsh with Krishna, since her resentment hurts only herself, and to go to him.
hinduism.explanation: The poem portrays a lover’s anger as a pose that melts away when faced with the beloved’s return.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine admits the same: the anger her heart shows her husband is false and would vanish at the sight of him.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the poem’s mana episode, not verified live this session; close on the lover’s sulk dissolving, though Radha’s anger rests on real jealousy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:”
christianity.explanation: Paul allows that anger arises but insists it must not be held on to.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees that her anger toward her husband cannot and should not last, for it is not real.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a loose ethical parallel on not prolonging anger, with nothing of the Kural’s playful lovers’ quarrel.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who spend [in the cause of Allah] during ease and hardship and who restrain anger and who pardon the people - and Allah loves the doers of good;”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those who hold back their anger and forgive.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine recognises that her anger toward her husband is hollow and gives way at once to love.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a general virtue of restraining anger, not a parallel to a lover’s feigned sulk.

judaism.quote_or_event: In the Song of Songs, the woman at first makes excuses not to open the door to her beloved, but her heart is moved for him and she rises to open, only to find he has gone.
judaism.explanation: Her show of reluctance gives way immediately to longing once she senses him near.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine likewise knows her reluctance and anger are a pose that her heart cannot keep up when the beloved is near.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase checked against the JPS 1917 text on Sefaria; good match on feigned reluctance melting into longing, though there is no explicit anger.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who checks rising anger as a charioteer checks a rolling chariot, him I call a true charioteer. Others only hold the reins.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha praises the person who can stop anger the moment it arises.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees that her anger toward her husband is not even worth reining in, for it is false and gives way at the sight of him.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a loose parallel on anger that does not run its course; the Kural’s anger is playful, not a defilement.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasant things (by themselves) do not cause indifference nor emotions (as anger, &c.); but by either hating or loving them, a man undergoes such a change through delusion.”
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching traces both love and anger to the same root of delusion, so that one easily turns into the other.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees that her anger at her husband is only the other face of her love, and so is not real anger at all.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi, Lecture 32); an analytical rather than narrative match, and Jainism would treat both love and anger as bondage.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Troy fell, Menelaus came upon Helen intending to kill her for her betrayal, but at the sight of her beauty he let his sword fall and took her back.
greek_mythology.explanation: In this well-known tradition, the husband’s anger cannot survive the sight of the woman he loves.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine knows her anger is equally hollow and would collapse the moment she saw her husband.
greek_mythology.source: Euripides, Andromache c. 627-631; cf. Aristophanes, Lysistrata 155-156 (paraphrase)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a widely attested episode, not verified live; line numbers approximate. A strong match on anger melting at the beloved’s sight, though with the roles of husband and wife reversed.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca argues that anger is not a natural necessity but a choice of the mind, which can be checked at its first stirring by reason.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, anger exists only because the mind assents to it, and so it can be dissolved.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees through her own anger in just this way: it is a pose her heart has adopted, not something real.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the treatise’s general argument, not verified live; a conceptual parallel only, since Seneca condemns anger rather than describing lovers’ sulks.

kurals.tamil:
காமம் விடுஒன்றோ நாண்விடு நன்னெஞ்சே
யானோ பொறேன்இவ் விரண்டு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaamam viduondroa naanvidu nannenjae
yaanoa poraen-iv virandu.
kurals.meaning: My good heart, either give up your desire or give up your modesty; I cannot bear both of them at once.
kurals.elementary: Imagine wanting very badly to tell someone how much you miss them, but feeling too shy to say it. Holding both feelings at once is hard, so you tell yourself, “Either stop missing them, or stop being shy and just tell them!”
kurals.university: This is the chapter’s best-known dilemma: kāmam viṭu oṉṟō (‘either let go of desire’) nāṇ viṭu (‘or let go of modesty’), for yāṉō poṟēṉ iv iraṇṭu (‘I cannot bear these two together’). Nāṇ (modesty, shame) is a defining virtue of the Tamil heroine, which normally forbids her from going to the man or declaring her longing; kāmam here means love-desire, not merely physical lust. The heart is called naṉṉeñcu (‘good heart’), a coaxing address. Kalaignar makes the conflict explicit (desire drives her to speak, modesty stops her), and Pappaiah stresses that the two pull in opposite directions; Pope renders it ‘Or bid thy love, or bid thy shame depart’. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When the gopis of Vraja hear Krishna’s flute at night, they abandon their household duties and the restraints of family and propriety, and hurry to meet him in the forest.
hinduism.explanation: In the Bhagavata’s account, love for Krishna overpowers the gopis’ sense of social shame.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine faces the same choice between love and modesty; the gopis resolve it by letting modesty go.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode, not verified live this session; verse range approximate. Strong match on love overriding shame, though the context is devotional.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For that which I do I allow not: for what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes a self torn between two opposing pulls that he cannot reconcile.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is likewise torn between two forces, desire and modesty, and finds she cannot bear both.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a parallel on an inwardly divided self, but Paul’s conflict is between sin and the law, not love and modesty.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet, passing a man who was admonishing his brother for being too modest, told him to leave him, for modesty (haya’) is part of faith.
islam.explanation: Islamic teaching holds modesty to be an essential virtue, not a weakness to be overcome.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine feels modesty as a real value even while love presses her to abandon it.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from knowledge of a well-known hadith, not verified live this session; it explains the weight of modesty but not its conflict with love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Oh that thou wert as my brother, That sucked the breasts of my mother! When I should find thee without, I would kiss thee; Yea, and none would despise me.”
judaism.explanation: The woman of the Song wishes she could show her love openly without incurring public shame.
judaism.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s dilemma: love wants to show itself, but modesty and fear of reproach hold it back.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a strong match on the tension between love and social shame.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that two bright qualities, hiri (moral shame) and ottappa (fear of wrongdoing), protect the world; without them, people would lose all restraint.
buddhism.explanation: In Buddhism, a sense of shame is a guardian virtue that keeps desire in check.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine feels the pull of this guardian, modesty, against her desire, and cannot bear both.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a standard teaching, not verified live; it explains the value of shame but not the heroine’s painful conflict.

jainism.quote_or_event: “…all these manifold passions arise in him who is attached to pleasures; and so do other emotions produced by those (before mentioned) arise in him who is to be pitied, who (ought to be) ashamed of himself, and who is hateful.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain text lists the many passions, including fear and sorrow, that spring up in one attached to pleasures, leaving him a figure of shame.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine feels desire and shame at war within her; the Jain answer would be to let go of desire, not modesty.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi, Lecture 32, final clause); weak next-best match: it links desire with shame but has no real dilemma, and Jainism would resolve it by renunciation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Medea, falling in love with Jason, spends a sleepless night torn between shame (aidōs) and love: her modesty and loyalty to her father hold her back, while love drives her to help the stranger.
greek_mythology.explanation: Apollonius gives a famous portrait of a young woman divided between modesty and passion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is precisely the Kural’s dilemma: the heroine cannot carry both love and modesty and begs her heart to drop one.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from knowledge of the poem, not verified live; line range approximate. A near one-to-one match on shame warring with love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s image of the soul as a chariot, one horse is restrained by modesty and shame, while the other is driven by desire toward the beloved, and the charioteer is pulled painfully between them.
philosophy.explanation: Plato pictures the lover’s soul as divided between a horse of shame and a horse of desire.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine experiences exactly this divided pull between modesty and desire, and finds it unbearable.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from knowledge of the passage, not verified live; a close structural match on shame and desire pulling in opposite directions.

kurals.tamil:
பரிந்தவர் நல்காரென்று ஏங்கிப் பிரிந்தவர்
பின்செல்வாய் பேதைஎன் நெஞ்சு.
kurals.transliteration:
Parindhavar nalkaarendru aengip pirindhavar
pinselvaai paedhaien nenju.
kurals.meaning: My foolish heart, you pine that he will not come back in pity and be kind to us, and yet you go running after the one who has left us.
kurals.elementary: Imagine saying, “My friend doesn’t care about me!” and then running after that same friend anyway. You might laugh at yourself: “Silly heart, you complain about them and then follow them everywhere!”
kurals.university: The heart is again called pētai (‘simpleton’), now for a contradiction: it laments (ēṅki) that the husband, out of pity (parintu), nalkār (‘will not show favour’), yet it goes piṉ cel (‘following behind’) the one who has pirintavar (‘parted’). Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the line as exposing the heart’s inconsistency; Solomon Pappaiah gives the more sympathetic reading that the heart follows him to tell him of her suffering, which he simply does not know. The verb nalku (‘to bestow grace, be kind’) is a key word of Tamil love poetry, often used of the hero’s favour to the heroine. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Krishna suddenly vanishes from the rasa dance, the gopis wander through the forest searching for him, asking the trees and creepers whether they have seen him pass.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata portrays lovers who, though left behind, cannot stop following the one who has gone.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heart likewise runs after the husband who has left, even while complaining that he shows no kindness.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known chapter, not verified live this session; strong match on following a departed beloved.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone: my soul failed when he spake: I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.”
christianity.explanation: The bride seeks and calls after a beloved who has withdrawn and does not answer.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heart, too, goes after one who has left and gives no response to its longing.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a strong match on pursuing a withdrawn, unresponsive beloved.

islam.quote_or_event: In Nizami’s romance, Majnun, separated from Layla, leaves everything behind and wanders the desert in pursuit of her, though she cannot come to him.
islam.explanation: The poem portrays a lover whose heart follows the beloved wherever she has gone, regardless of reason.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heart, called foolish, likewise follows the one who has parted from it.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous romance from the Islamic literary tradition, not scripture; not verified live. Close on the foolish heart that follows.

judaism.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth; I sought him, but I found him not. ’I will rise now, and go about the city, In the streets and in the broad ways, I will seek him whom my soul loveth.’ I sought him, but I found him not.”
judaism.explanation: The woman of the Song rises at night and goes out through the city in search of her absent beloved.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heart, too, cannot stay still but goes after the one who has gone away.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a strong match on following an absent beloved, without the Kural’s note of self-reproach.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Wonderful, indeed, it is to subdue the mind, so difficult to subdue, ever swift, and seizing whatever it desires. A tamed mind brings happiness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the untamed mind as swift and always rushing after what it wants.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heart behaves exactly so, rushing after the departed husband against the heroine’s own judgment.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; matches the runaway heart, though the Buddha’s concern is taming the mind, not love.

jainism.quote_or_event: When Prince Ariṣṭanemi (Neminatha) renounced the world on his wedding day and went up Mount Raivataka, his bride Rājīmatī, overwhelmed with grief, cut off her hair, became a nun, and herself set out for Mount Raivataka.
jainism.explanation: The Jain story shows a forsaken bride following the one who left her, though along the path of renunciation.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heart likewise follows the one who has parted from it, though Rājīmatī’s following is spiritual, not romantic.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase checked against Jacobi’s text on sacred-texts.com; a close narrative image of following the departed, transformed by Jainism into renunciation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After losing Eurydice, Orpheus follows her down into the underworld itself, unable to accept being parted from her.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows a lover who will follow the beloved even beyond the limits of the living world.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heart, too, follows the one who has left, even though doing so is called foolish.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous myth, not verified live; Eurydice is dead rather than unwilling, so the fit is on following, not on indifference.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Symposium, Aristophanes tells how humans were split in two, and how each half now searches for and runs after its other half, longing to be reunited.
philosophy.explanation: The myth explains love as the restless pursuit of the missing part of oneself.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heart, following the one who has parted from it, enacts just this pursuit of the missing half.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from knowledge of the speech, not verified live; a strong account of love as pursuit, without the Kural’s self-reproach.

kurals.tamil:
உள்ளத்தார் காத லவரால் உள்ளிநீ
யாருழைச் சேறியென் நெஞ்சு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ullaththaar kaadha lavaraal ulli-nee
yaaruzhaich cheriyaen nenju.
kurals.meaning: My heart, our beloved lives right here inside you; so, thinking of him, to whom are you going out to look for him?
kurals.elementary: Imagine searching the whole house for your favourite toy while holding it in your hand the whole time. The Kural says the same to the heart: “The person you miss is already inside you, why go looking for them outside?”
kurals.university: The heroine catches her heart in a paradox: kātalavar uḷḷattār āl (‘the beloved is in the heart’, with āl as an emphatic particle), so when nī uḷḷi (‘you, thinking of him’) set off, yār uḻai cēṟi (‘to whom will you go?’; uḻai = ‘to the side of, to the place of’). Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it as ‘to whom do you go searching, when he is within?’; Pope gives ‘Roaming, whom dost thou think to find?’. The line is a rare moment of consolation in the chapter, and has often been read devotionally, the beloved dwelling in the heart being a common image in Tamil bhakti. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (ytamizh prints a spaced kāta lavarāl).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The Supreme Lord is situated in everyone’s heart, O Arjuna, and is directing the wanderings of all living entities, who are seated as on a machine, made of the material energy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that the One whom beings seek already dwells within their own hearts.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine realises the same of her beloved: he lives inside her heart, so there is nowhere outside to search.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.61 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com; the ‘beloved within the heart’ image fits, though the Gita speaks of the Lord as indwelling controller, not a human lover.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Neither shall they say, Lo here! or, lo there! for, behold, the kingdom of God is within you.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his hearers not to look for the kingdom here or there, for it is already within them.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural similarly tells the heart not to go searching outside for the one who already lives inside it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a close parallel on not seeking outside what is within, though the object is the kingdom of God.

islam.quote_or_event: “And We have already created man and know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than [his] jugular vein”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says God is nearer to a person than their own life-vein, so there is no need to seek Him far away.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine discovers that her beloved, too, is nearer than anywhere her heart might wander to find him.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a strong ‘nearer than you think’ parallel, though about God, not a lover.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Set me as a seal upon thy heart, As a seal upon thine arm; For love is strong as death, Jealousy is cruel as the grave; The flashes thereof are flashes of fire, A very flame of the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved asks to be pressed into the heart like a seal, a permanent mark within.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s beloved already is such a seal: he dwells in the heroine’s heart, so the heart need not seek him elsewhere.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); close on the beloved imprinted in the heart, though the Song does not rebuke a searching heart.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Dwelling in the cave (of the heart), the mind, without form, wanders far and alone. Those who subdue this mind are liberated from the bonds of Mara.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the mind as dwelling in the heart yet constantly wandering far away.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heart behaves just so: its beloved lives inside it, yet it wanders off to search for him.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a vivid image of a mind that lives within but roams outside, though the aim is to subdue it, not to rest in a beloved.

jainism.quote_or_event: Kundakunda teaches that the pure soul is to be found and known within oneself, by turning inward, and that seeking it among outward things is a delusion.
jainism.explanation: Digambara mysticism insists that what one truly seeks is found within, not in external objects.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural tells the heart a similar truth about its beloved, who already dwells within, though Jainism would point to the self rather than a lover.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a central Samayasara theme without a specific verse, not verified live; only the ‘seek within’ structure matches, and the object differs entirely.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Laodamia, whose husband Protesilaus was killed at Troy, kept a likeness of him in her chamber and devoted herself to it as if he were still present.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows a wife keeping her absent husband present to herself through an image she holds close.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine keeps her husband present in her heart, which makes any outward search unnecessary.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested myth, not verified live; the beloved kept close fits, but Laodamia’s image is outward, not within the heart.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Too late did I love You, O Fairness, so ancient, and yet so new! Too late did I love You! For behold, You were within, and I without, and there did I seek You”
philosophy.explanation: Augustine confesses that he searched outside himself for the One he loved, who was all the while within him.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine catches her heart making the same mistake: running outside to seek a beloved who lives within.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on newadvent.org (Pilkington translation); a near one-to-one structural match on seeking outside the beloved who is within, though Augustine’s beloved is God.

kurals.tamil:
துன்னாத் துறந்தாரை நெஞ்சத்து உடையேமா
இன்னும் இழத்தும் கவின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thunnaath thurandhaarai nenjaththu udaiyaemaa
innum izhaththum kavin.
kurals.meaning: If we keep in our heart the one who left us and does not come near, we will lose even more of the beauty we have left.
kurals.elementary: Imagine thinking all day about a friend who went away and never visits. The more you think about it, the more tired and sad you look. So you tell yourself, “If I keep holding on like this, I’ll lose even more of my sparkle.”
kurals.university: The closing couplet weighs the cost of constancy: tuṉṉāt tuṟantārai (‘him who, not drawing near, has left us’; tuṉṉu ‘to approach, be joined’, tuṟa ‘to leave, renounce’) neñcattu uṭaiyēmā (‘if we hold in the heart’), iṉṉum iḻattum kaviṉ (‘we shall lose still more of our beauty’). Kaviṉ is beauty or comeliness, linking back to chapter 124 on the wasting of the limbs. Solomon Pappaiah draws out the force of iṉṉum (‘still more’): having already lost her outer beauty, she will now lose her inner beauty too, a reading echoed in Pope’s ‘further loss of dignity’. The line ends the soliloquy on the heroine’s awareness that her loyalty is consuming her, without any resolve to give it up. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “While contemplating the objects of the senses, a person develops attachment for them, and from such attachment lust develops, and from lust anger arises.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna traces how continually dwelling on an object in the mind deepens attachment and leads to ruin.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees the same pattern in herself: by keeping the absent man in her heart, she is wearing herself away further.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.62 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com; fits the harm of dwelling on the beloved in thought, though the Gita’s chain runs to anger and delusion rather than loss of beauty.

christianity.quote_or_event: “My heart is smitten, and withered like grass; so that I forget to eat my bread.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist describes grief so deep that his heart withers and he neglects even to eat.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine, holding on to the man who left, is likewise withering and losing what beauty she has left.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a close physical image of wasting from sorrow, though not caused by an absent lover.

islam.quote_or_event: “In order that you not despair over what has eluded you and not exult [in pride] over what He has given you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an counsels believers not to be consumed by grief over what has passed out of their reach.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees that clinging to one who has left her is consuming her, the very despair this verse warns against.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih), first sentence only; a general counsel against grief over loss, not about love specifically.

judaism.quote_or_event: “’Stay ye me with dainties, refresh me with apples; For I am love-sick.’”
judaism.explanation: The woman of the Song says her love has made her literally faint and ill.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine, too, is being worn down in body by the love she keeps in her heart.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); matches love-sickness, but in the Song the beloved is near, not one who has left.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From craving springs grief, from craving springs fear. For one who is wholly free from craving there is no grief; whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that holding on to what one craves is the source of grief.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine recognises that holding the departed man in her heart is what keeps her grieving and wasting.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it diagnoses her condition, though it proposes a detachment she does not choose.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When the daughter of the king heard of the ordination of the Jina, laughter and gaiety forsook her, and she was overwhelmed with affliction. Rājīmatī thought: ‘Shame upon my life, that I have been forsaken by him! it is better I should turn nun.’”
jainism.explanation: Rājīmatī, abandoned on her wedding day when Neminatha renounced the world, loses all her joy, then turns her grief into renunciation.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, she is forsaken by the one who ‘renounced’ (tuṟantār), and her gaiety drains away.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi, Lecture 22; diacritics normalised); a strong match on the forsaken bride losing her joy, though Rājīmatī turns to renunciation rather than holding him in her heart.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Spurned by Narcissus, Echo wastes away with sleepless care: her body grows thin, her beauty dries up, and at last only her voice and bones remain.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid shows a lover literally consumed by holding on to one who will not return her love.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine foresees the same fate: keeping the departed man in her heart will strip away what beauty she has left.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage, not verified live; line numbers approximate. A near match on beauty wasting from unreturned love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius warns that love is a wound that festers and grows worse the more it is fed, and advises the lover to stop feeding it with images of the absent beloved before it becomes incurable.
philosophy.explanation: Lucretius sees dwelling on the beloved’s image as the very thing that makes love’s sickness worse.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine comes to the same realisation: holding him in her heart only deepens her loss.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from knowledge of the passage, not verified live; line numbers approximate. A strong match on love worsening as it is nursed in the mind.
